claims.text: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr is the alloy system being modeled.
The modeled states include an ideal defect-free crystal and a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed machine-learning model integrates molecular-dynamics and density-functional-theory data with experimental conductivity measurements.
The simulation data capture defect and oxygen-impurity scattering.
The integrated model will predict electrical transport more accurately than analytical models based on perfect crystals.
The integrated model will predict thermal transport more accurately than analytical models based on perfect crystals.
Quantum scattering dominates transport from nearly 0 K to 200 K.
Localization effects may be important from nearly 0 K to 200 K.
Phonon scattering and defect interactions are significant from 300 K to 1200 K.
A 1 wt.% oxygen content induces transport-relevant defect interactions in the high-temperature regime.
Descriptors for defect density, oxygen distribution, and scattering parameters mediate the modeled relationship between microstructure and transport.
The model learns nonlinear correlations among temperature, defect and impurity features, and transport behavior.
Exposure to realistic scattering mechanisms in training data enables more accurate conductivity interpolation than a perfect-lattice analytical model.
Conductivity predictions for pristine and 1 wt.% oxygen specimens will be within ±5% of experiment in both stated temperature regimes.
Traditional analytical predictions typically differ from experiment by more than ±15%.
Traditional analytical models assume defect-free crystals and omit impurity scattering.
The claimed accuracy advantage applies from nearly 0 K through 1200 K and to oxygen contents up to 1 wt.%.
Accuracy may degrade outside the stated temperature and oxygen-content limits.
Prediction accuracy depends on the quality and breadth of the simulation and experimental training data, and unmodeled mechanisms or rare defects may increase error.
A prediction error greater than ±5% at either approximately 150 K for pristine material or approximately 800 K for oxygen-doped material will falsify the hypothesis.
